notes.2: (i) In this question, candidates needed to demonstrate that they understood the requirements for a mapping to be a function. Some candidates realised that graph B represented a function. Not as many realised that graph C also represented a function. The simplest correct reason given was that each x value gives only one y value. A few candidates stated that these graphs passed the vertical line test, which was also acceptable. A few good candidates stated that C was a function in part (i) , with an acceptable reason and stated B was a function that had an inverse in part (ii) , with an acceptable reason. These candidates had omitted to notice that, as B was a function that had an inverse, it was also a function and should have been included in their answer to part (i) . Some candidates thought that graph D also represented a function, although very few chose graph A. Those candidates choosing B, C and D usually justified their choice by stating that these graphs continued to infinity and were not closed, like A. Some candidates were attempting to describe the graphs rather than give a reason to explain why each of their choices was a function. Some were, for example, stating that graph B was ‘a cubic’ and graph C was ‘an absolute value’ graph. Neither of these were correct justification for why these graphs represented functions. A very small number of candidates thought all four graphs represented functions. These candidates had not recalled the correct condition for a mapping to be a function, as they usually stated that all four had input and output. (ii) Here, candidates needed to show that they understood that, for a function to have an inverse, it must be one-to-one. Some candidates stated a correct reason but selected C rather than B. Other candidates chose graphs on the basis that they could be reflected in the line y = x , which was not correct thinking. Many candidates seemed to be making choices based on the symmetry of the graph.

notes.8: (i) A very good number of correct answers were seen. Some candidates observed that the sector was of the circle, using the information given as expected, and quickly found both the angle and the radius using this approach. Other candidates arrived at the correct values using longer methods. This was fine, although it did introduce a greater possibility of making an error. Some candidates needed to take care to read and interpret the information in the question more carefully. It was possible to work out the value of θ and r independently. Some candidates may have done better if they had observed this. A few candidates correctly marked the length of the major arc as 10 π and 2 π then treated this as the circumference. This resulted in the answers r = 5 and θ = , which were seen on occasion. Very weak candidates incorrectly stated their angles in degrees. (ii) A good number of candidates earned both marks. Some good candidates were not awarded the accuracy mark as they omitted to give their final answer in exact form as required. Re-reading the question may have helped these candidates. All candidates should be aware that answers in exact form often involve values which have components that are multiples of π , as was the case for this question. Some candidates need to understand that exact values will not be found using rounded decimals for the value of θ . Candidates who observed that the triangle AOB was equilateral had much less work to do than those who used the cosine rule to find the length of the chord AB . (iii) Once again, many candidates applied a correct strategy and earned all the marks available. Some candidates omitted to give their answer in exact form in this part also and were penalised. Here the exact form had a component that was a multiple of π as well as a surd. Again, this is often the case when exact answers are requested. In order to give an exact answer, exact values must be used throughout the calculation and this is good mathematical practice. Weaker candidates sometimes used calculations that were not dimensionally correct, mixing lengths and areas.
notes.9: (i) In order to find the inverse function, candidates needed to apply a correct order of inverse operations and swop the variables at some point. The domain of the inverse function was also required. Many good candidates did all of this and were rewarded with full marks. Some candidates omitted to state the domain. These may have benefited from re-reading the question to make sure they had completed it. Other candidates had an incorrect order of operations or applied an incorrect inverse operation, such as square-rooting where squaring was required, or did not state their final answer in terms of x . A few candidates attempted to find the domain and made errors. The most common of these were stating x ⩾ 0, f > 0, x > 1 or x = ℝ . (ii) Again, candidates needed to state their answer in exact form. In this case, the answer should be a surd. Very many candidates earned 2 marks, understanding the requirement for an exact answer. Answers stated in decimal form only were penalised. Most candidates successfully found g(7) and then found f(51). Those few candidates who formed the composite function first occasionally made errors when doing so. A few candidates would have done better to have used their calculator to evaluate g(7), as 16 was stated as its value on occasion.
